title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1RC0LF_0LD0RC_1RA1LE_---1LA_0LC1LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1RC0LF_0LD0RC_1RA1LE_---1LA_0LC1LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 107 steps; the C simulator finds none in 1011.
Reduced to one machine. Lean proves this is 1RB1LE_1RC1LD_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LB_0LD1LF with renamed states, started in state B. See that machine for the mechanism.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 152 cells have been visited and 99 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c runs 100,000,000,000 steps without a halt; the head reached 189 cells on the left side and 174 on the right (record positions).

claims.title: M3 is T with its states renamed
claims.text: 1RB1LC_1RC0LF_0LD0RC_1RA1LE_---1LA_0LC1LF is 1RB1LE_1RC1LD_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LB_0LD1LF with the states renamed A→D, B→A, C→B, D→C (every transition, halts included), so its run from blank tape is the run of 1RB1LE_1RC1LD_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LB_0LD1LF started in state B on blank tape: one 1 fewer at the left than T's own run after its first step. m3_iff.

claims.title: T and M1 make the same run until a 0 sits within two cells left of A reading a 1
claims.text: The two machines differ only in the 1-transitions of A, B and E, which all write 1 and move left. The seven-state machine S = 1RB1LE_1RC---_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LG_0LD1LF_---1LD is the part they share (B split into B entered from A0 and E entered from A1). Every step S makes, both make on the same tape (shadow); in S, B entered from A0 always reads a 0, because A is entered only by D0 = 0LA (star_good); so S stops only where A has read a 1 and then meets a 0 one cell (S's E0) or two cells (S's G0) further left, and there exactly one of T and M1 halts and the other goes on with B0 = 1RC (deviation). Hence S halts iff T or M1 halts (star_halts_iff), and if neither halts they make the same run step for step (same_run).

claims.title: T and M1 agree for the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: S runs 107 steps from blank tape without stopping (and 10,000 checked by the kernel), so by shadow the two machines have the same tape and head at each of those steps.

claims.title: T and M1 agree for the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs S for 10<sup>11</sup> steps without a stop; with the Lean simulation theorem this means the two machines make the same run through 10<sup>11</sup> steps (which is why their record outputs were identical).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts iff T started in state B halts (proved); the rules of T's higher counter levels are not known, so there is no argument either way.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB1LE_1RC1LD_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LB_0LD1LF up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 152 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Three holdouts, one machine
html: Three holdouts of this group have the same tape shape, and Lean proves why. Call T = 1RB1LE_1RC1LD_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LB_0LD1LF. The holdout 1RB1LC_1RC0LF_0LD0RC_1RA1LE_---1LA_0LC1LF is T with its states renamed; started on blank tape it is T started in state B instead of A, which only removes one 1 at the left edge. The holdout M1 = 1RB1LB_1RC1LE_1RD0LF_0LA0RD_---1LD_0LD1LF differs from T in what A, B and E do on a 1; all of these write a 1 and move left, so the two can only part when A has read a 1 and then meets a 0 one or two cells further left. At that moment one of them halts and the other goes on. Until then (and the C simulator shows this does not happen in 1011 steps) they make exactly the same run.

In S, E is "B entered from A1" and G is "what comes after". M1 is S with E read as B and G as E; T is S with G read as B. S halts on E0 exactly where T halts and on G0 exactly where M1 halts.

sections.heading: This page's machine is T started in B
html: This machine is T with renamed states, started in T's state B. Its run is T's run from a slightly different start, so it has the same counters with different contents; everything said here about T's mechanism applies, but the epoch numbers above are for T's own run.

sections.heading: The only way to halt: 0, 1, 0
html: T halts only when E reads a 0. E comes only from A reading a 1, A only from D reading a 0, and D reading a 0 can only lead there if D moved left onto that 0 (from F reading 0 or B reading 1) with a 1 and then a 0 further left. Lean proves the exact statement: the run halts iff it ever has F reading 0, or B reading 1, with 0 1 0 just to the left of the head. In 2·109 steps this never happens; F stops at a 0 next to 1 1 0 or 0 1 1 only 15 times, all early.

sections.heading: Counters inside counters
html: The digits are 3-cell blocks: 000 is a 0 and 111 a 1. The left part of the tape is a binary counter written this way, split into sections that each begin with a 111 and are separated by a single blank cell. A small region in the middle, where the head spends nearly all its time, adds 1 to the counter at a perfectly regular rate. A snapshot at step 10,000,794 (dots are 0s, F is the head):

When the whole counter is at all ones it is a single run of 1s reaching the left edge. The head then runs over it to the left end, wipes it, and the counter starts again from zero with one more digit. So the time between these visits doubles: each epoch has 2k counts. Each epoch also changes a short tail at the right end once, and every few epochs the long runs of 1s in the middle (unary numbers such as 122, then 116, then 110) are rewritten: a third level of counting.

sections.heading: The clock is exact
html: Within each stretch of the run, every count costs exactly the same number of steps on average, so the epoch lengths double exactly:
At step 98,851,039,064 the counter has 29 digits. The changes between stretches come from the higher levels, whose rules are not known.

sections.heading: What would settle it
html: A halt needs the pattern 0 1 0 where the head turns, which the low-level counter never produces. Whether a higher level ever produces it depends on rules that have not been decoded: how the middle unary numbers and the tail change at each stretch boundary. With those rules one could write the run as a map on a few numbers and either prove it never makes the pattern or find when it does. Until then there is no heuristic either way.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
